title: blastFoam Theory and User Guide

text:
blastFoam is an open-source toolbox for simulating detonations based on the OpenFOAM ®1 framework (OpenCFD Ltd., 2018a). blastFoam provides solutions to highly compressible systems including single- and multi-phase compressible flow, including single- and multi-velocity systems, based on the work of Zheng et al. (2011), Shyue (2001), and Houim and Oran (2016). blastFoam provides implementations of the essential numerical methods (e.g. 2nd and 3rd order schemes), equations of state (e.g. ideal gas, stiffened gas, Jones-Wilkins-Lee, etc.), run-time selectable flux schemes (e.g. HLL, HLLC, AUSM+, Kurganov/Tadmor), and high-order explicit time integration (e.g. 2nd, 3rd, and 4th order). blastFoam provides activation and explosive burn models to simulate the initiation and expansion of energetic materials, as well as afterburn models to simulate under-oxygenated explosives that exhibit delayed energy release.

> 1DISCLAIMER: This offering is not approved or endorsed by OpenCFD Limited, producer and distributor of the OpenFOAM software via www.openfoam.org, and owner of the OpenFOAM and OpenCFD trade marks.

title: blastFoam Theory and User Guide Contents

text:
blastFoam is an opensource computational fluid dynamics (CFD) code based on the OpenFOAM C++ library (OpenCFD Ltd., 2018a) to simulate strongly compressible systems of equations with detonations. Along with the main solvers for simulating fluid flow, additional utilities have been added to simplify case setup, allow adaptive mesh refinement with load balancing based on the work of Rettenmaier et al. (2019), and facilitate blastFoam specific case post-processing.

The purpose of this guide is to serve as a reference for the governing equations and the models that have been implemented in blastFoam. The guide also provides a brief description of the capabilities of the solver and the new utilities that have been introduced on top of those available in the standard OpenFOAM. Many of the available models include options that the user can tune to best suit their simulations, and are given in a table at the end of each model description.
title: Introduction

text:
blastFoam currently builds against OpenFOAM-9 2. The following dependencies are required to successfully compile and run blastFoam:

1. A working installation of OpenFOAM-9 complete with libraries and headers produced by OpenFOAM-9, no other packages are required to run blastFoam applications. If OpenFOAM-9 is compiled from source, the ThirdParty-9 repository source is also required. If a pre-compiled version of OpenFOAM-9 is used, this is automatically installed.

2. In order to create and view the postscript plots (e.g. `*.eps` files), gnuplot is available on all platforms. EPS Viewer can be used on Windows and ghostview can be used on linux. On macOS, Preview opens eps files natively.

2https://github.com/OpenFOAM/OpenFOAM-9
title: Introduction System Requirements

text:
The un-compiled source code can be obtained at: https://github.com/synthetik-technologies/blastfoam. Download or clone the source in the following location: `$HOME/OpenFOAM/blastfoam`

```sh
mkdir -p $HOME/OpenFOAM # create the OpenFOAM directory
cd $HOME/OpenFOAM # go to the directory
git clone https://github.com/synthetik-technologies/blastfoam
```
title: Introduction Downloading

text:
After cloning the the blastFoam source code from https://github.com/synthetik-technologies/blastfoam (see previous section) and installing any optional libraries, similar to OpenFOAM, add the following line to `$HOME/.bashrc` file:

```sh
source ~/OpenFOAM/blastfoam/etc/bashrc
```

and run:

```sh
source ~/.bashrc
```

in any open terminals to update the BASH environment. This is used to specify the local directories included during blastFoam compilation, as well as make future developments easier and less intrusive.

Next run the `./Allwmake` command from the top blastFoam directory to compile the libraries and applications. Finally, ensure that OpenFOAM-9 and blastFoam have been installed and that the environment has been correctly setup by running one of the tutorial or validation cases.

Summary of steps to download, configure and compile blastFoam:

```sh
# 1. create the OpenFOAM directory if if does not exist
mkdir -p $HOME/OpenFOAM
# 2. go to the $HOME/OpenFOAM directory
cd $HOME/OpenFOAM
# 3. # clone the blastFoam repository
git clone https://github.com/synthetik-technologies/blastfoam
# go to the blastfoam directory
cd $HOME/OpenFOAM/blastfoam
# Source the etc/bashrc to your .bashrc file
# by runngin the following command in terminal
echo "source $HOME/OpenFOAM/blastfoam/etc/bashrc" >> $HOME/.bashrc
# Re-load and set the bash environment to compile blastFoam
source $HOME/.bashrc
# Compile blastFoam (for parallel use "-j")
./Allwmake
```
title: Introduction Compilation

text: The applications to solve these equations are executed by running the executable name (i.e. `blastFoam`). The executables are stored within the `$BLAST_APPBIN` (`$FOAM_USER_APPBIN` by default but this can be overridden) directory and can be run from any directory.

title: Introduction Getting Help

text:
Here the governing conservation equations used within blastFoam will be described.

We will describe two cases: (1) the single-fluid case where a single shared velocity and energy is used and (2) the multi-fluid case where each fluid has a unique velocity and energy. The phrase "multi-phase" will be used to denote a fluid that uses multiple equations of states to describe the density-energy-pressure relation.

For both variations $U$ is the vector of conservative variables, $F$ are the fluxes corresponding to the respective conservative variables, and $S$ is a vector of source terms,

$$
∂_t U + ∇ · F = S
$$

(2.1)

The exact form each of these take will depend on whether the single-fluid or multi-fluid is used. Each of these are presented in the following sections.
title: Governing equations

text:
For a single phase with multiple species, the conservative variables and fluxes are defined as

$$
U = \begin{pmatrix} ρ \\ ρ Y_s \\ ρu \\ ρE \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.2)

$$
F = \begin{pmatrix} ρu \\ ρ Y_s u \\ ρu ⊗ u + pI \\ (ρE + p)u \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.3)

$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \dot{R}_s + ∇ · J_s \\ \dot{M} + \dot{M}_v \\ \dot{E} + \dot{E}_v \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.4)

where $Y_s$ is the mass fraction of specie $s$, and $J_s$ is the diffusion flux of species $s$. For multiple phases

$$
U = \begin{pmatrix} α_1 \\ \vdots \\ α_n \\ α_1 ρ_1 \\ \vdots \\ α_n ρ_n \\ ρu \\ ρE \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.5)

$$
F = \begin{pmatrix} α_1 u \\ \vdots \\ α_n u \\ α_1 ρ_1 u \\ \vdots \\ α_n ρ_n u \\ ρu ⊗ u + pI \\ (ρE + p)u \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.6)

$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} α_1 ∇ · u \\ \vdots \\ α_n ∇ · u \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ \dot{M} + \dot{M}_v \\ \dot{E} + \dot{E}_v \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.7)

where $ρ$ is the mixture density, $u$ is the mixture velocity, $E$ is the total energy (thermal and kinetic), $p$ is the pressure, and $ρ_i$ and $α_i$ are the density and volume fraction of each phase.

The source terms, $\dot{R}_s$, $\dot{M}$, and $\dot{E}$ are the specie production from reactions, momentum, and energy sources (including gravitational acceleration), and $\dot{M}_v$ and $\dot{E}_v$ are viscous terms.

The sum of all volume fractions is defined to be one, i.e.

$$
\sum_i α_i = 1
$$

(2.8)

When only two phases are used, the second volume fraction is defined

$$
α_2 = 1 − α_1
$$

(2.9)

Additionally, the mixture density is defined by

$$
ρ = \sum_i α_i ρ_i
$$

(2.10)

When all phases are considered inviscid, $\dot{M}_v = \dot{E}_v = 0$. However, when viscosity is included,

$$
\dot{M}_v = ∇ · \left( ρν \left[ ∇u + (∇u)^⊺ − \frac{2}{3}(∇ · u)I \right] \right)
$$

(2.11)

and

$$
\dot{E}_v = ∇ · \left( ρν \left[ ∇u + (∇u)^⊺ − \frac{2}{3}(∇ · u)I \right] · u \right) + ∇ · (α_T ∇e)
$$

(2.12)

where $ν$ is the viscosity, $α_T$ is the thermal diffusivity, and $I$ is the identity matrix.

The five equation model is used for multiphase systems in which a single shared velocity, a shared internal energy and temperature is used, and individual phase masses are conserved. Pressure is defined using a specified EOS, where the mixture's internal energy, densities, and volume fraction are used to calculate the total pressure.
title: Governing equations 2.1 Single-fluid model

text: Similar to flows that use a single shared velocity and energy, the mass, momentum, and energy are all conserved. In contrast, however, each phase has its own set of mass, momentum, and energy, which is transferred between phases using interfacial transfer models (such as drag, heat transfer, etc.).
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid

text:
The conservation equations for the $i$th fluid phase are

$$
U_i = \begin{pmatrix} α_i \\ α_i ρ_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i E_i \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.13)

$$
F = \begin{pmatrix} α_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i ⊗ u_i + α_i p_i I \\ α_i (ρ_i E_i + p_i) u_i \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.14)

$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} α_i ∇ · u_i + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} I(ρ_i, ρ_j) \\ \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} \\ α_i ρ_i g + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{M}_{ij} + \dot{M}_{v,i} \\ α_i ρ_i g · u_i + \sum_{i \ne j} (\dot{E}_{ij} + \dot{M}_{ij} · u_{int,ij}) + \dot{E}_{det,i} + \dot{E}_{v,i} \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.15)

where $α_i$ is the phase volume fraction, $ρ_i$ is the phase density, $u_i$ is the phase velocity, $E_i$ is the total phase energy, and $p_i$ is the phase pressure. The source terms, $\dot{M}_{ij}$ and $\dot{E}_{ij}$, are the momentum and energy sources that account for interactions between other phases, $\dot{M}_{v,i}$ and $\dot{E}_{v,i}$ are viscous terms, $g$ is the gravitational acceleration vector, $\dot{E}_{det,i}$ is the energy added due to reactions, and $u_{int,ij}$ is the interfacial velocity between two phases. When mass transfer is used $\dot{ω}_{i,j}$ is the mass transfer rate from the $i$th phase to the $j$th phase, and $I$ is a switching function used to select the transferring quantity (Xue et al., 2011) and is defined as

$$
I(x_i, x_j) = ξ_{i,j} x_j + (1 − ξ_{i,j}) x_i
$$

(2.16)

and

$$
ξ_{i,j} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \dot{ω}_{i,j} > 0 \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}
$$

(2.17)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid

text:
The viscous stress uses a Newtonian stress tensor defined as

$$
\dot{M}_{v,i} = ∇ · \left( α_i ρ_i ν_i \left[ ∇u_i + (∇u_i)^⊺ − \frac{2}{3}(∇ · u_i)I \right] \right)
$$

(2.18)

and

$$
\dot{E}_{v,i} = ∇ · \left( α_i ρ_i ν_i \left[ ∇u_i + (∇u_i)^⊺ − \frac{2}{3}(∇ · u_i)I \right] · u_i \right) + ∇ · (α_i α_{T,i} ∇e_i)
$$

(2.19)

where $ν_i$ is the viscosity, $α_{T,i}$ is the thermal diffusivity, and $I$ is the identity matrix.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid

text:
The momentum transfer term, $\dot{M}_{ij}$, is defined as

$$
\dot{M}_{ij} = \dot{M}_{D,ij} + \dot{M}_{L,ij} + \dot{M}_{VM,ij} + \dot{M}_{WL,ij} + \dot{M}_{TD,ij} + \dot{ω}_{i,j} I(u_i, u_j)
$$

(2.20)

where the summed terms, in order, represent drag, lift, virtual mass, wall lubrication, and turbulent dispersion, respectively.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid

text:
The energy transfer term, $\dot{E}_{ij}$, is defined as

$$
\dot{E}_{ij} = \dot{E}_{HT,ij} + \dot{ω}_{i,j} I(E_i, E_j + hf_i − hf_j)
$$

(2.21)

where $\dot{E}_{HT,ij}$ is the energy transfer rate due to convective heat transfer, and $hf$ is the heat of formation.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid

text:
In contrast to a standard fluid (gas or liquid), a granular fluid tracks the phase mass, momentum, thermal energy, and granular energy. The last quantity, granular energy, is the energy that is present due to fluctuation in the phase velocity within a cell. This is the kinetic energy due to the local velocity variance. The more common quantity is the granular temperature, $Θ_i$, which is related to the granular energy by $⟨E⟩_i = \frac{3}{2} Θ_i$. The governing equations are

$$
U_i = \begin{pmatrix} α_i ρ_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i e_i \\ α_i ρ_i ⟨E⟩_i \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.22)

$$
F = \begin{pmatrix} α_i ρ_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i ⊗ u_i + (P_{s,i} + P_{fric,i})I \\ α_i ρ_i e_i u_i \\ α_i ρ_i u_i ⟨E⟩_i \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.23)

$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} \\ α_i ρ_i g − α_i \sum_{\ell} ∇p_{int,i\ell} + \sum_j \dot{M}_{ij} + \dot{M}_{v,i} \\ \sum_j \dot{e}_{ij} + \sum_k \dot{γ}_{ik} + \dot{e}_{det,i} \\ −\sum_k \dot{γ}_{ik} − \sum_{\ell} φ_{prod,i\ell} − P_{s,i} ∇ · u_i + α_i τ_i : ∇u_i + ∇ · (κ_{s,i} ∇Θ_i) + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} I(⟨E⟩_i, 0) \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.24)

where, again, $α_i$ is the phase volume fraction, $ρ_i$ is the phase density, $u_i$ is the phase velocity, and $e_i$ is the phase thermal energy. The summations $\sum_j$, $\sum_k$, and $\sum_{\ell}$ denote summations over all phases, all solid phases, and all fluid phases, respectively. The new quantities, $P_{s,i}$, $P_{fric,i}$, $⟨E⟩$, and $p_{int}$ are the granular pressure, frictional pressure, granular energy, and interfacial pressure (generally taken as the gas phase pressure), respectively. The density is assumed to be constant, so the volume fraction is found by simply dividing the total phase mass by the known density. The source terms, $\dot{M}_{ij}$, $\dot{e}_{ij}$, $\dot{γ}_{ij}$, and $φ_{prod,il}$ are the momentum transfer, energy transfer, granular energy dissipation, and production terms. The momentum and energy transfer terms are the same as for a fluid phase ($\dot{e}_{ij} = \dot{E}_{ij}$ and $\dot{e}_{det,i} = \dot{E}_{det,i}$). The production and dissipation terms are described below.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
The production and dissipation of granular energy introduce a new term into the continuous phase total energy equation so that the continuous phase source terms become

$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} α_i ∇ · u_i + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} I(ρ_i, ρ_j) \\ \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{ω}_{ij} \\ α_i ρ_i g + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{M}_{ij} + \dot{M}_{v,i} \\ α_i ρ_i g · u_i + \sum_{i \ne j} \dot{E}_{ij} + \dot{E}_{det,i} + \dot{E}_{v,i} + \sum_k φ_{prod,k} \\ \sum_k \dot{ω}_{ik} I(0, ⟨E⟩_k) \end{pmatrix}
$$

(2.25)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text: You can also see in Eq. (2.22) that the dissipation of granular energy is converted into thermal energy within the solid phase. For those familiar with incompressible flows, this term is typically neglected due to the fact that the amount of heat produced from collisions is typically very small. In highly compressible flows, this is not the case, and significant heat can be generated due to the loss of energy from inelastic collisions.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
We define the change in momentum due to granular phase stress as

$$
\dot{M}_{ij} = ∇ · τ_{s,i} + \dot{ω}_{i,j} I(u_i, u_j)
$$

(2.26)

and the granular stress is defined as

$$
τ_{s,i} = ρ_i ν_{s,i} [∇u_i + (∇u_i)^⊺] + \left( λ_{s,i} − \frac{2}{3} ρ_i ν_{s,i} \right) (∇ · u_i)I
$$

(2.27)

with $λ_{s,i}$ being the bulk viscosity of the granular phase defined by (Huilin and Gidaspow, 2003)

$$
λ_{s,i} = \sum_k \left( \frac{P_{s,ik}}{d_{ik}} \right) 3 \sqrt{\frac{2(m_i Θ_i + m_k Θ_k)^2}{π Θ_i Θ_k (m_i^2 Θ_i + m_k^2 Θ_k)}}
$$

(2.28)

where $P_{s,ij}$ is the granular pressure between solid phases $i$ and $k$, and is related to $P_{s,i}$ by

$$
P_{s,i} = α_i ρ_i Θ_i + \sum_k P_{s,ik}
$$

(2.29)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
The production of granular energy is given by

$$
φ_{prod,i\ell} = \frac{81 α_i µ_{\ell}^2 g_{0,ii}}{d_i^3 ρ_i \sqrt{π}} \frac{|u_{\ell} − u_i|^2}{\sqrt{Θ_i}} − 3 K_{D,i\ell} Θ_i
$$

(2.30)

where $K_{D,i\ell}$ is the drag coefficient for the $i$-$\ell$ solid-fluid pair and $g_{0,ij}$ is the radial distribution function.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
The dissipation of granular energy between granular phases $i$ and $k$ is defined by (Huilin and Gidaspow, 2003)

$$
\dot{γ}_{ik} = \left[ \frac{3}{d_{ik}} \sqrt{\frac{2 m_0^2 Θ_i Θ_k}{π(m_i^2 Θ_i + m_k^2 Θ_k)}} − \frac{3 m_0 (m_i Θ_i + m_k Θ_k)}{4(m_i^2 Θ_i + m_k^2 Θ_k)} ∇ · u_i \right] (1 − e_{ik}) P_{s,ik}
$$

(2.31)

where

$$
m_i = \frac{ρ_i π d_i^3}{6}
$$

(2.32)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text: $d_{ik} = (d_i + d_k)/2$, $m_0 = m_i + m_k$, $e_{ik}$ is the coefficient of restitution between granular phases $i$ and $j$, and $P_{s,ik}$ is the granular pressure between phases $i$ and $k$. The drag, radial distribution function, and granular pressure are determined by models and will be discussed in Sec. 3.1 and Sec. 4. The specific manner as to how these source terms are solved can be found in Appendix B.7 of Houim and Oran (2016).
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
The energy transfer term, $\dot{e}_{ij}$, is defined as

$$
\dot{e}_{ij} = \dot{e}_{HT,ij} + \dot{ω}_{i,j} I(e_i, e_j + hf_i − hf_j)
$$

(2.33)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
Lastly, the speed of sound for a granular material is given by

$$
c_i^2 = \frac{1}{ρ_i} \left[ \frac{∂P_{tot,i}}{∂α_i} + \frac{2}{3} Θ_i \frac{\left( \frac{∂P_{tot,i}}{∂Θ_i} \right)^2}{ρ_i α_i^2} \right]
$$

(2.34)

where $P_{tot,i} = P_{s,i} + P_{fr,i}$. Because different models can be used for the granular pressure, frictional pressure, and additional models used within radial distribution functions, the specific form this takes is not discussed here.
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text: The topic of granular flows, or kinetic theory, is quite extensive and thus it would be impractical to attempt to provide complete descriptions and derivations of the equations and models discussed here. For more more details on this topic, the reader should consult the following resources:
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
- For derivations relating to molecular gasses, see Chapman et al. (1990)
- For more practical derivations, see Gidaspow (1994)
- For applications to compressible flows, see Fox (2019)
- For derivations of the polydisperse formulations, see Huilin and Gidaspow (2003) and Chao et al. (2011)
title: Governing equations 2.2 Multi-fluid 2.2.1 Granular phases

text:
The exchange of momentum and energy is determined by the use of interfacial models. These models are described below and include the equations used to calculate the transfer rates. In general, these models are solved using an explicit Euler integration method. Drag and heat transfer, however, are solved using an analytical solution; the reference used for these solution methods will be provided in the relevant sections.

NOTE: There are more models currently implemented that do not apply to gas-particle flows and, therefore, are not presented at this time. Their descriptions and equations will be added as they become relevant.
title: Interfacial models

text:
The drag is responsible for relaxing the velocity difference between two phases to an equilibrium velocity at a rate determined by the drag coefficient, $K_{D,ij}$:

$$
K_{D,ij} = \frac{0.75\alpha_d C_D Re_{ij}\rho_c \nu_c}{d_d^2}
$$
(3.1)

where the Reynolds number between phases $i$ and $j$ is defined as $Re_{ij} = \frac{d_d|u_c - u_d|}{\nu_c}$. The subscripts $c$ and $d$ are used to denote the continuous and dispersed phases, respectively. The term $C_D Re_{ij}$ will be defined by the models discussed in the following sections.

The momentum transfer term is defined as $\dot{M}_{D,ij} = K_{D,ij}(u_j - u_i)$. The solution to the drag relaxation can be found in Appendix B.7 of Houim and Oran (2016). Additionally, an ODE solver can be used to solve the drag relaxation, though this approach is much more computationally expensive.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| swarmCorrelation | Swarm model |
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models

text:
The drag model of Schiller and Naumann (1933) calculates the drag coefficient for flow over a single sphere:

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = \begin{cases} 24(1 + 0.15Re_{ij}^{0.687}) & \text{if } Re_{ij} < 1000 \\ 0.44Re_{ij} & \text{else} \end{cases}
$$
(3.2)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualRe | Minimum Reynolds number [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.1 SchillerNaumann

text:
The Wen and Yu drag model (Enwald et al., 1996) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is defined as

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = C_D Re_{sSN,ij}\alpha_c^{-2.65}
$$
(3.3)

where $C_D Re_{sSN,ij}$ is the Schiller Naumann drag coefficient multiplied by the Reynolds number, and the Reynolds number used in the drag coefficient is weighted by the dispersed phase volume fraction, i.e.,

$$
Re_{s,ij} = Re_{ij}\alpha_c
$$
(3.4)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualRe | Minimum Reynolds number [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.2 WenYu

text:
The Ergun drag model (Enwald et al., 1996) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is defined as

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = \frac{4}{3}\frac{150(1 - \alpha_c)}{\alpha_c} + 1.75Re_{ij}
$$
(3.5)
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.3 Ergun

text:
The Gibilaro drag model (Enwald et al., 1996) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is defined as

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = \frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{17.3}{\alpha_2} + 0.336Re_{ij}\right)\alpha_c\alpha_2^{-2.8}
$$
(3.6)

where $\alpha_2 = 1 - \alpha_d$.
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.4 Gibilaro

text:
The Syamlal O'Brien drag model (Syamlal et al., 1993) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is defined as

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = \frac{C_{Ds}Re_{ij}\alpha_c}{V_r^2}
$$
(3.7)

where

$$
C_{Ds}Re_{ij} = \left(0.63\sqrt{Re_{ij}} + 4.8\sqrt{V_r}\right)^2
$$
(3.8)

$$
V_r = 0.5\left(A - 0.06Re_{ij} + \sqrt{(0.06Re_{ij})^2 + 0.12Re_{ij}(2B - A) + A^2}\right)
$$
(3.9)

$$
A = \alpha_2^{4.14}
$$
(3.10)

$$
B = \begin{cases} 0.8\alpha_2^{1.28} & \text{if } \alpha_2 < 0.85 \\ \alpha_2^{2.65} & \text{else} \end{cases}
$$
(3.11)

and $\alpha_2 = 1 - \alpha_d$.
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.5 SyamlalOBrien

text:
The drag model of Gidaspow (1994) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is a combination of the Wen and Yu drag model (dilute) and Ergun drag model (dense):

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = \begin{cases} C_D Re_{WenYu,ij} & \text{if } \alpha_c > 0.80 \\ C_D Re_{Ergun,ij} & \text{else} \end{cases}
$$
(3.12)

where $C_D Re_{WenYu,ij}$ is the Wen Yu drag coefficient and $C_D Re_{Ergun,ij}$ is the Ergun drag coefficient, both multiplied by the Reynolds number.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualRe | Minimum Reynolds number [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.6 GidaspowErgunWenYu

text:
The Gidaspow-Schiller Naumann drag model (Enwald et al., 1996) is used for dispersed particulate flow and the drag coefficient is defined as

$$
C_D Re_{ij} = C_{Ds}Re_{ij}\alpha_c^{-1.65}
$$
(3.13)

$$
C_{Ds}Re_{ij} = \begin{cases} \frac{24(1 + 0.15Re_{s,ij}^{0.687})}{\alpha_c} & \text{if } Re_{s,ij} < 1000 \\ 0.44Re_{s,ij} & \text{else} \end{cases}
$$
(3.14)

where the Reynolds number used in the drag coefficient is weighted by the dispersed phase volume fraction, i.e.,

$$
Re_{s,ij} = Re_{ij}\alpha_c
$$
(3.15)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualRe | Minimum Reynolds number [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.1 Drag models 3.1.7 GidaspowSchillerNaumann

text:
The lift interfacial momentum transfer model is used to account for acceleration due to rotation in the continuous phase and is defined as

$$
\dot{M}_{L,ij} = C_{L,ij}\alpha_d\rho_c\left[(u_c - u_i)\times(\nabla\times u_c)\right]
$$
(3.16)

where $C_{L,ij}$ is the lift coefficient between phases $i$ and $j$ and is defined by the model of choice.
title: Interfacial models 3.2 Lift models

text:
The lift coefficient is a constant value.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Cl | Lift coefficient [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.2 Lift models 3.2.1 constant

text:
The heat transfer model is responsible for relaxing the temperature between two phases at a rate determined by the model of choice. The Prandtl number will be used and is defined as

$$
Pr_{ij} = \frac{\nu_c C_{vc}\rho_c}{\kappa_c}
$$
(3.17)

Again, the subscripts $c$ and $d$ represent the continuous and dispersed phases, respectively. $C_{vc}$ is the continuous phase specific heat at constant volume and $\kappa_c$ is the continuous phase thermal conductivity. The solution to the temperature relaxation can be found in Appendix B.7 of Houim and Oran (2016).
title: Interfacial models 3.3 Heat transfer models

text:
The Ranz Marshall heat transfer model (Houim and Oran, 2016) defines the heat transfer rate as

$$
\dot{E}_{HT,ij} = \frac{6\alpha_d\kappa_c Nu_{ij}}{d_d^2}
$$
(3.18)

where the Nusselt number is a run-time selectable model, and all other properties are taken from the thermodynamic model.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| NuModel | Nusselt number model |
| residualAlpha | Stabilization value of volume fraction (defaults to that of the phaseModel) |
title: Interfacial models 3.3 Heat transfer models 3.3.1 RanzMarshall

text: This should only be used is a Nusselt number is needed by some other model, but heat transfer is neglected.
title: Interfacial models 3.3 Heat transfer models 3.3.2 noneNu

text:
For the constant Nusselt number heat transfer model, Eq. (3.18) is again used, but the Nusselt number is a constant value provided by the user.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Nu | Nusselt number [ ] |
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.1 constant

text:
For hollow particles the Nusselt number of Dittus and Boelter (1930) is defined as

$$
Nu_{ij} = 0.023Re_{ij}^{0.8}Pr_{ij}^{0.4}
$$
(3.19)
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.2 duct

text:
The Nusselt number of Gelperin and Einstein (1971) is defined as

$$
Nu_{ij} = 0.023Re_{ij}^{2/3}Pr_{ij}^{1/3}
$$
(3.20)
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.3 GelperinEinstein

text:
The Nusselt number of Gunn (1978) is defined as

$$
Nu_{ij} = (7 - 10\alpha_c + 5.0\alpha_c^2)(1 + 0.7Re_{ij}^{0.2}Pr_{ij}^{1/3}) + (1.33 - 2.4\alpha_c + 1.2\alpha_c^2)Re_{ij}^{0.7}Pr_{ij}^{1/3}
$$
(3.21)
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.4 Gunn

text:
The Ranz-Marschall Nusselt number for spheres is defined as

$$
Nu_{ij} = 2 + 0.6Re_{ij}^{1/2}Pr_{ij}^{1/3}
$$
(3.22)
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.5 RanzMarschall

text:
The Nusselt number for spheres is defined as

$$
Nu_{ij} = 2 + 0.4Re_{ij}^{1/2}Pr_{ij}^{1/3}
$$
(3.23)
title: Interfacial models 3.4 Nusselt number models 3.4.6 sphere

text: Currently on particle to fluid mass transfer has been implemented. Fluid-fluid mass transfer is not currently supported.
title: Interfacial models 3.5 Mass transfer models
Interfacial models 3.5 Mass transfer models 3.5.1 none

text: The mass transfer rate is explicitly calculated using the change in mass of a particle where the regression rate is determined by a reaction rate. the reactingParticle diameter model must be used.
title: Interfacial models 3.5 Mass transfer models 3.5.2 reactingParticle

text: The interfacial pressure model is used to determine the pressure at the interface between two phases.
title: Interfacial models 3.6 Interfacial pressure models

text:
The pressure of the given phase is used.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| phase | Name of the phase |

NOTE: For gas-particle flows this option should be used, using the gas phase pressure.
title: Interfacial models 3.6 Interfacial pressure models 3.6.1 single

text: The volume fraction averaged pressure of the two phases is used.
title: Interfacial models 3.6 Interfacial pressure models 3.6.2 volumeAveraged

text: The volume fraction averaged thermodynamic pressure and the mass averaged dynamic pressure is used.
title: Interfacial models 3.6 Interfacial pressure models 3.6.3 totalPressure

text: The interfacial velocity model is used to determine the velocity at the interface between two phases.
title: Interfacial models 3.7 Interfacial velocity models

text:
The velocity of the given phase is used.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| phase | Name of the phase |

NOTE: For gas-particle flows this option should be used, using the particle phase velocity.
title: Interfacial models 3.7 Interfacial velocity models 3.7.1 single

text: The mass averaged velocity of the two phases is used.
title: Interfacial models 3.7 Interfacial velocity models 3.7.2 massAveraged

text:
For granular phases, additional models are required to account for particle-particle collisions in both the kinetic and frictional regimes. These models include radial distribution, viscosity, conductivity, granular pressure, frictional pressure, solid-solid drag, and packing models.

Some common variables used in the granular models will now be defined. Here, $P_k$ is the summation over all granular phase indices and $α_s$ is the sum of all granular phase volume fractions. The strain is defined as

$$
S = \frac{1}{2}\left[(∇u)^{⊺} + ∇u\right] - \frac{1}{3}(∇·u)I
$$
(4.1)

The symmetric strain is defined as

$$
D = \frac{1}{2}\left[(∇u)^{⊺} + ∇u\right]
$$
(4.2)

Finally, the total granular drag on a phase is defined as

$$
K_{D,i} = \sum_k K_{D,ik}
$$
(4.3)
title: Granular models

text: The radial distribution gives the likelihood of a collision between two particles. This is defined between like and unlike particle phases.
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models

text:
The Carnahan Starling radial distribution function is only valid for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
g_{0,ii} = \frac{1}{1-α_i} + \frac{3α_i}{2(1-α_i)^2} + \frac{α_i^2}{2(1-α_i)^3}
$$
(4.4)
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models 4.1.1 CarnahanStarling

text:
The radial distribution of Sinclair and Jackson (1989) function is only valid for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
g_{0,ii} = \frac{1}{1-\left(\frac{α_i}{α_{i,max}}\right)^{1/3}}
$$
(4.5)
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models 4.1.2 SinclairJackson

text:
The radial distribution function of Lun et al. (1984) is only valid for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
g_{0,ii} = \left(1-\frac{α_i}{α_{max,i}}\right)^{-2.5α_{max,i}}
$$
(4.6)
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models 4.1.3 LunSavage

text:
The radial distribution function of Gao et al. (2008) is a modified version of the Sinclair Jackson radial distribution function and is valid for polydisperse flows. It is defined as

$$
g_{0,ij} = \frac{d_i g_{0,i} + d_j g_{0,j}}{d_i + d_j}
$$
(4.7)

$$
g_{0,i} = \frac{1}{1-\left(\frac{α_i}{α_{i,max}}\right)^{1/3}}
$$
(4.8)
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models 4.1.4 Gao

text:
The Lebowitz radial distribution function (Benyahia et al., 2012) is valid for polydisperse flows and is defined as

$$
g_{0,ij} = \frac{1}{1-α_s} + \frac{3d_i d_j}{(1-α_s)^2(d_i+d_j)}\sum_k\frac{α_k}{d_k}
$$
(4.9)
title: Granular models 4.1 Radial distribution models 4.1.5 Lebowitz

text: The modeling of granular viscosity is used to determine the stress seen in a granular phase. These models only account for single collisions (frictional models will have additional contributions for multiple collisions).
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models

text:
The Gidaspow viscosity model (Gidaspow, 1994) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
ν_{s,i} = \frac{4}{5}α_i^2 g_{0,ii}\frac{(1+e_{ij})}{π} + \frac{1}{15}\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}(1+e_{ii})α_i^2 + \frac{1}{6}\sqrt{π}α_i + \frac{10}{96}\sqrt{π}(1+e_{ii})g_{0,ii}
$$
(4.10)
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models 4.2.1 Gidaspow

text:
The Hrenya Sinclair viscosity model (Hrenya and Sinclair, 1997) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
ν_{s,i} = \frac{4}{5}α_i^2 g_{0,ii}\frac{(1+e_{ij})}{π} + \frac{1}{15}\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}(3e_{ii}-1)\frac{α_i^2}{3-e_{ii}} + \frac{1}{6}\frac{\sqrt{π}α_i(0.5λ+0.25(3e_{ii}-1))}{0.5(3-e_{ii})λ} + \frac{10}{96}\frac{\sqrt{π}}{(1+e_{ii})0.5(3-e_{ii})g_{0,ii}λ}
$$
(4.11)

where

$$
λ = 1 + \frac{d_i L}{6\sqrt{2α_i}}
$$
(4.12)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| L | characteristic length [m] |
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models 4.2.2 HrenyaSinclair

text:
The Princeton viscosity model (Agrawal et al., 2001) is for polydisperse flows and is defined as

$$
ν_{s,i} = ρ_i\frac{3.6}{3}\left[\frac{µ_i^*}{g_{0,ii}η(2-η)}\left(1+\frac{8}{5}η\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})\right)\times\left(1+\frac{8}{5}η(3η-2)\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})\right)+\frac{3}{5}ηµ_b\right]
$$
(4.13)

where

$$
µ_i^* = \frac{ρ_iα_i g_{0,ii}Θ_i µ}{ρ_i\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})Θ_i + \frac{2K_{d,i}µ}{ρ_iα_i}}
$$
(4.14)

$$
µ = \frac{5}{96}ρ_i d_i\sqrt{πΘ_i}
$$
(4.15)

and

$$
µ_b = \frac{256}{5π}µα_i\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})
$$
(4.16)
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models 4.2.3 Princeton

text:
The Syamlal viscosity model (Syamlal et al., 1993) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
ν_{s,i} = \frac{4}{5}α_i^2 g_{0,ii}\frac{(1+e_{ii})}{π} + \frac{1}{15}\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}(3e_{ii}-1)\frac{α_i^2}{3-e_{ii}} + \frac{1}{6}\frac{\sqrt{π}α_i}{3-e_{ii}}
$$
(4.17)
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models 4.2.4 Syamlal

text: No granular viscosity is used. This also removes the conductivity contribution to the granular energy equation.
title: Granular models 4.2 Granular viscosity models 4.2.5 none

text:
The Chao granular conductivity model Chao et al. (2011) is defined as

$$
κ_{s,i} = \frac{2κ_{dilute,i}}{\frac{1}{N}\sum_k(1+e_{ik})g_{0,ik}}\left[1+\frac{6}{5}\sum_kα_k(1+e_{ik})g_{0,ik}\right]^2
$$
(4.18)

where N is the number of granular phases and

$$
κ_{dilute,i} = \frac{15ρ_iΘ_i}{\sum_k\left(\frac{π}{\sqrt{2π}n_k d_{ij}^2(\sqrt{Θ_i}+\sqrt{Θ_j}-0.56\sqrt[4]{Θ_iΘ_j})}\right)}
$$
(4.19)
title: Granular models 4.3 Granular conductivity models 4.3.1 Chao

text:
The Gidaspow conductivity model (Gidaspow, 1994) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
κ_{s,i} = \frac{2α_i^2 g_{0,ii}(1+e_{ii})}{\sqrt{π}} + \frac{9}{8}\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}0.5(1+e_{ii})α_i^2 + \frac{15}{16}\sqrt{π}α_i + \frac{25}{64}\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}(1+e_{ii})
$$
(4.20)
title: Granular models 4.3 Granular conductivity models 4.3.2 Gidaspow

text:
The Hrenya Sinclair conductivity model (Hrenya and Sinclair, 1997) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
κ_{s,i} = \frac{2α_i^2 g_{0,ii}(1+e_{ii})}{\sqrt{π}} + \frac{9}{8}\frac{\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}0.25(1+e_{ii})^2(2e_{ii}-1)α_i^2}{\frac{49}{16}-\frac{33}{16}e_{ii}} + \frac{15}{16}\frac{\sqrt{π}α_i(0.5e_{ii}^2+0.25e_{ii}-0.75+λ)}{(\frac{49}{16}-\frac{33}{16}e_{ii})λ} + \frac{25}{64}\frac{\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}λ(1+e_{ii})}{\frac{49}{16}-\frac{33}{16}e_{ii}}
$$
(4.21)

where

$$
λ = 1 + \frac{d_i L}{6\sqrt{2α_i}}
$$
(4.22)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| L | characteristic length [m] |
title: Granular models 4.3 Granular conductivity models 4.3.3 HrenyaSinclair

text:
The Princeton conductivity model (Agrawal et al., 2001) is for polydisperse flows and is defined as

$$
κ_{s,i} = \frac{κ_i^*}{g_{0,ii}}\left[\left(1+\frac{12}{5}η\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})\right)\left(1+\frac{12}{5}η^2(4η-3)\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})\right)+\frac{64}{25π}(41-33η)η^2\left(\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})\right)^2\right]
$$
(4.23)

where

$$
κ_i^* = \frac{ρ_iα_i g_{0,ii}Θ_i κ_i}{ρ_i\sum_k(α_k g_{0,ik})Θ_i + \frac{6K_{d,i}κ_i}{5ρ_iα_i}}
$$
(4.24)

and

$$
κ_i = \frac{75ρ_i d_i\sqrt{πΘ_i}}{48η(41-33η)}
$$
(4.25)
title: Granular models 4.3 Granular conductivity models 4.3.4 Princeton

text:
The Syamlal conductivity model (Syamlal et al., 1993) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
κ_{s,i} = \frac{2α_i^2 g_{0,ii}(1+e_{ii})}{\sqrt{π}} + \frac{9}{8}\frac{\sqrt{π}g_{0,ii}0.25(1+e_{ii})(2e_{ii}-1)α_i^2}{\frac{49}{16}-\frac{33}{16}e_{ii}} + \frac{15}{16}\frac{\sqrt{π}α_i}{\frac{49}{16}-\frac{33}{16}e_{ii}}
$$
(4.26)
title: Granular models 4.3 Granular conductivity models 4.3.5 Syamlal

text: The granular pressure model is used to calculate the pressure due to single collisions between particles. Pressures that occur due to multiple collisions will be added using the frictional models.
title: Granular models 4.4 Granular pressure models

text:
The Huilin granular pressure model (Huilin and Gidaspow, 2003) is for polydisperse flows and is defined as

$$
P_{s,ij} = \frac{π(1+e_{ij})d_{ij}^3 g_{0,ij}n_i n_j m_i m_j m_0 Θ_i Θ_j}{3(m_i^2 Θ_i + m_j^2 Θ_j)}\times\left[\frac{m_0^2 Θ_i Θ_j}{(m_i^2 Θ_i + m_j^2 Θ_j)(Θ_i+Θ_j)}\right]^{3/2}\times(1-3ω+6ω^2-10ω^3)
$$
(4.27)

with

$$
ω = \frac{m_i Θ_i - m_j Θ_j}{\left[(m_i^2 Θ_i^2 + m_j^2 Θ_j^2)+Θ_i Θ_j(m_i^2+m_j^2)\right]^{1/2}}
$$
(4.28)
title: Granular models 4.4 Granular pressure models 4.4.1 Huilin

text:
The Lun granular pressure model (Lun et al., 1984) is for monodisperse flows and is defined as

$$
P_{s,ij} = α_i α_j ρ_i Θ_i 2(1+e_{ij})g_{0,ij}
$$
(4.29)
title: Granular models 4.4 Granular pressure models 4.4.2 Lun

text: The frictional stress model acts as a simple way to account for non-singular collisions between particles and results in very large stress when the granular phases approach their packing limit. This results in both a modeled pressure and viscosity to calculate a stress, and limits the ability of particles to move between computational cells. The frictional pressure and viscosity denoted $P_{fr}$ and $ν_{fr}$ act on all granular phases since the packing of particles is dependent on the total volume fraction of particles.
title: Granular models 4.5 Frictional stress models

text:
The Johnson-Jackson frictional stress model (OpenCFD Ltd., 2018b) uses a smooth function to calculate the pressure

$$
P_{fr} = \begin{cases}\frac{F_r(α_s-α_{crit,s})^{η}}{(α_{max,s}-α_s)^{p}} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.30)

and the frictional viscosity is

$$
ν_{fr} = 0.5P_{fr}\sin(φ)
$$
(4.31)

where φ is the angle of internal friction, and $F_r$, η, and p are model coefficients generally taking values of 0.05, 2, and 5 respectively. $α_{crit,s}$ is the granular particle fraction that the frictional pressure "turns on", and $α_{max,s}$ is the maximum packing limit of all granular phases. Generally $α_{crit,s}$ is taken to be around 0.5.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Fr | Model coefficient [ ] |
| eta | Model coefficient [ ] |
| p | Model coefficient [ ] |
| phi | Model coefficient [ ] |
| alphaDeltaMin | Minimum value of $α_s - α_{max,s}$ [ ] |
| alphaMinFriction | Volume fraction friction is "turned on" [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.5 Frictional stress models 4.5.1 JohnsonJackson

text:
The Schaeffer frictional stress model (Syamlal et al., 1993) uses a power law and the local stress is used to calculate the frictional viscosity. The critical volume fraction, $α_{crit,s}$ should be a value close to that of the packing limit. Because the local packing limit can vary in space when polydispersity is present, the ratio of the local volume fraction by the critical volume fraction is used, i.e. $α_{crit,s} = \left(\frac{α_{crit,s}}{α_{max,s}}\right)_{crit}α_{max,s}$ where $\left(\frac{α_{crit,s}}{α_{max,s}}\right)_{crit}$ is specified by the user and $α_{max,s}$ is the calculated local packing limit. The pressure is defined as

$$
P_{fr} = \begin{cases}1024(α_s-α_{crit,s})^{10} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.32)

and the viscosity is

$$
ν_{fr} = \begin{cases}\frac{0.5P_{fr}\sin(φ)}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}(I_1(D)^2-I_2(D))}} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.33)

where $I_1(D)$ is the first invariant (or trace) and $I_2(D)$ is the second invariant.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| phi | Model coefficient [ ] |
| alphaMinFrictionByAlphap | Volume fraction ratio friction is "turned on" [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.5 Frictional stress models 4.5.2 Schaeffer

text:
For the Johnson Jackson-Schaeffer frictional stress model (OpenCFD Ltd., 2018b), the frictional pressure of Johnson Jackson is used while the viscosity of the Schaeffer model is used.

$$
P_{fr} = \begin{cases}\frac{F_r(α_s-α_{crit,s})^{η}}{(α_{max,s}-α_s)^{p}} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.34)

$$
ν_{fr} = \begin{cases}\frac{0.5P_{fr}\sin(φ)}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}(I_1(D)^2-I_2(D))}} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.35)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Fr | Model coefficient [ ] |
| eta | Model coefficient [ ] |
| p | Model coefficient [ ] |
| phi | Model coefficient [ ] |
| alphaDeltaMin | Minimum value of $α_s - α_{max,s}$ [ ] |
| alphaMinFriction | Volume fraction friction is "turned on" [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.5 Frictional stress models 4.5.3 JohnsonJacksonSchaeffer

text:
The Princeton model Agrawal et al. (2001) uses a blending of the Johnson Jackson model when the local volume fraction is greater than $α_{crit,JJ,s}$ but less than $α_{crit,Sc,s}$. As with the Schaeffer model, the critical ratio of $\left(\frac{α_{crit,Sc,s}}{α_{max,s}}\right)_{crit}$ is used as an input rather than $α_{crit,Sc,s}$.

$$
P_{fr} = \begin{cases}1024(α_s-α_{crit,Sc,s})^{10} & \text{if } α_s > α_{crit,Sc,s}\\\frac{F_r(α_s-α_{crit,JJ,s})^{η}}{(α_{max,s}-α_s)^{p}} & \text{if } α_{crit,Sc,s} ≤ α_s > α_{crit,JJ,s}\\0 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.36)

The frictional viscosity is defined using

$$
\frac{P_{c,k}}{P_{fr}} = \left[1-\left(\frac{∇·u_s}{n\sqrt{2}\sin(φ)\sqrt{S:S+Θ_k/d_k^2}}\right)^{n-1}\right]
$$
(4.37)

$$
ν_{fr,k} = \frac{\sqrt{2}P_{c,k}\sin(φ)}{\sqrt{S:S+Θ_k/d_k^2}}\left[n-(n-1)\left(\frac{P_{c,k}}{P_{fr}}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-n}}\right]\frac{α_k}{α_s}
$$
(4.38)

and

$$
n = \begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2\sin(φ)} & \text{if } ∇·u_s ≥ 0\\1.03 & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.39)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| Fr | Model coefficient [ ] |
| eta | Model coefficient [ ] |
| p | Model coefficient [ ] |
| phi | Model coefficient [ ] |
| alphaDeltaMin | Minimum value of $α_s - α_{max,s}$ [ ] |
| alphaMinFriction | Volume fraction friction is "turned on" [ ] |
| alphaMinFrictionByAlphap | Volume fraction ratio friction is "turned on" [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.5 Frictional stress models 4.5.4 Princeton

text: The modeling of the packing limit is important in polydisperse flows due to the fact that, when large variations in particle diameters exist locally, the packing limit can vary widely. This is due to the fact that smaller particles can be found in between larger particles, increasing the maximum allowable volume fraction. For monodisperse flows, this is not the case and a constant value packing limit should be used.
title: Granular models 4.6 Packing limit models

text:
A constant value for the packing limit is used.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| alphaMax | Packing limit [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.6 Packing limit models 4.6.1 constant

text:
The Yu Standish packing model (Yu and Standish, 1987) assumes that the particle phases are ordered from smallest diameter to largest for the calculation of the packing limit. The packing limit is defined as

$$
α_{max,s} = \min_{i∈1:N}\left[\frac{α_{max,i}}{1-\sum_{k=1}^{i-1}\left(1-\frac{α_{max,i}}{p_{ik}}\right)\frac{cx_i}{X_{ik}}-\sum_{k=i+1}^{N}\left(1-\frac{α_{max,i}}{p_{ik}}\right)\frac{cx_i}{X_{ik}}}\right]
$$
(4.40)

where

$$
cx_i = \frac{α_i}{α_s}
$$
(4.41)

$$
X_{ik} = \begin{cases}\frac{1-r_{ik}^2}{2-α_{max,i}} & \text{if } k < i\\1-\frac{1-r_{ik}^2}{2-α_{max,i}} & \text{if } k ≥ i\end{cases}
$$
(4.42)

$$
p_{ik} = \begin{cases}α_{max,i}+α_{max,i}(1-α_{max,i})\times(1-2.35r_{ik}+1.35r_{ik}^2) & \text{if } r_{ik} ≤ 0.741\\α_{max,i} & \text{if } r_{ik} > 0.741\end{cases}
$$
(4.43)

and

$$
r_{ik} = \begin{cases}\frac{d_i}{d_k} & \text{if } i ≥ k\\\frac{d_k}{d_i} & \text{if } i < k\end{cases}
$$
(4.44)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualAlpha | Minimum volume fraction to divide by [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.6 Packing limit models 4.6.2 YuStandish

text:
The Fedors-Landel packing model (Fedors and Landel, 1979) is only valid of for a binary mixture and is defined as

$$
α_{max,s} = \begin{cases}\left[(α_{max,1}-α_{max,2})+(1-\sqrt{r_{21}}(1-α_{max,1})α_{max,2})\right]\times\left[α_{max,1}+(1-α_{max,1})α_{max,2}\right]\frac{cx_i}{α_{max,1}}+α_{max,2} & \text{if } cx_1 ≤ \frac{α_{max,1}}{α_{max,1}+(1-α_{max,1})α_{max,2}}\\\left(1-\sqrt{r_{21}}\right)\left[α_{max,1}+(1-α_{max,1})α_{max,2}\right]cx_2+α_{max,1} & \text{else}\end{cases}
$$
(4.45)

Where the definitions of $r_{21}$ and $cx_i$ are used from the previous section.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| residualAlpha | Minimum volume fraction to divide by [ ] |
title: Granular models 4.6 Packing limit models 4.6.3 FedorsLandel

text: The drag force between granular phases is different than standard drags models due to the fact the the collisions which are a function of the granular energy strongly effect the rate at which the velocities relax. These granular drag models are only necessary when multiple granular phases are used.
title: Granular models 4.7 Granular drag models

text:
The Chao granular drag model (Chao et al., 2011) defines the drag coefficient between phases as

$$
K_{D,ij} = \frac{α_iα_jρ_iρ_j}{m_0 d_{ij}(1+e_{ij})g_{0,ij}}\times\left[\sqrt{2π}(\sqrt{Θ_i}+\sqrt{Θ_j})-\sqrt{2}(Θ_iΘ_j)^{1/4}+0.5π|u_i-u_j|-1.135\sqrt{|u_i-u_j|}\left(\sqrt[4]{4Θ_i}+\sqrt[4]{Θ_j}-0.8\sqrt[8]{Θ_iΘ_j}\right)\right]
$$
(4.46)
title: Granular models 4.7 Granular drag models 4.7.1 Chao

text:
The Syamlal granular drag model (Benyahia et al., 2012) defines the drag coefficient between phases as

$$
K_{D,ij} = \frac{3(1+e_{ij})\left(\frac{π}{2}+\frac{C_{f,ij}π^2}{8}\right)α_iα_jρ_iρ_j(d_i+d_j)^2 g_{0,ij}|u_i-u_j|}{2π(ρ_i d_i^2+ρ_j d_j^3)}+C_1 P_{fr}
$$
(4.47)

where $C_{f,ij}$ is the coefficient of friction between granular phases i and j, and $C_1$ is the coefficient of frictional pressure.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| C1 | Coefficient of frictional pressure (default is 0) [s/m$^2$] |
title: Granular models 4.7 Granular drag models 4.7.2 Syamlal

text:
Within blastFoam solvers, two different types of basic thermodynamic models
are used. The primary is that of a fluid where internal energy and density, or
temperature and density, are used to find the resulting pressure and speed of
sound. The other, is the solid thermodynamic model, which is only used for
solid phases within multi-fluid solvers and multi-region solvers. These two
models will share the basic thermodynamic classes (eConst, hConst, etc),
as well as the choice in the type (basic, detonating, or multicomponent),
however the solid phase only can use a constant density equation of state,
and the transport model describes the of heat conduction, rather than flow
coefficients (like viscosity). These specific choices will be described below.
To calculate the pressure and temperature given the conservative quantities (mass, momentum, and energy) three components are required: an equation of state, a thermodynamic model, and a transport model. These models are defined in the `phaseProperties` file located in the `constant` directory of each blastFoam case. Each phase within the `phaseProperties` file has several dictionary entries, and these models are specified in the "thermoType" sub-dictionary; the molecular weight must also be defined in the "specie" sub-dictionary.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models
Fluid and solid thermodynamic models

text: > **NOTE:** Not all combinations of thermodynamic model, equation of state, transport, and mixture type are compiled, however using the dynamic compilation available in OpenFOAM, if a valid option is requested it will be compiled at run time and the library will be stored in the `dynamicCode` folder in the case. If any changes are made to the source code (updating/pulling) will not affect these libraries, and the `dynamicCode` folder will need to be removed for re-compilation.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models

text: > **NOTE:** By default, any thermodynamic combination that has not previously been compiled will be compiled using the files in `blastfoam/etc/codeTemplates`. These files include support for the standard model, however using the "templateDir" entry a different folder can be used, so that user modified files can be used. This allows for use of user implemented equations of state, thermodynamic, or transport models.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models

text:
The thermodynamic model is used to calculate the internal energy based solely on the thermal contribution:

$$
e_T = \int C_v(T)\,dT
$$
(5.1)

An additional contribution from the equation of state is given by:

$$
e_{eos}(\rho, T) = \int \left( T\frac{\partial p(\rho, T)}{\partial T} - p(\rho, T) \right) dv
$$
(5.2)

where $v_i = 1/\rho_i$ is the specific volume. The total internal energy is

$$
e = e_T(T) + e_{eos}(\rho, T)
$$
(5.3)

Because the internal energy is the tracked quantity, the temperature is solved using a Newton-Raphson root finding method given the local internal energy and density.

Either internal energy or enthalpy-based coefficients can be used, but only internal energy is used to define the total energy. The conversion from an enthalpy base to an internal energy base is calculated using the specified equation of state. All transport models, with the exception of the tabulated methods were ported from OpenCFD Ltd. (2018b).

$$
C_v = C_p - C_{pMCv}
$$
(5.4)

where $C_{pMCv}$ is determined from the equation of state using

$$
C_{pMCv} = \frac{\partial(p(\rho, e)v)}{\partial T}
$$
(5.5)

For an ideal gas, $C_{pMCv} = \bar{R}/W$ where $\bar{R}$ is the ideal gas constant (8314 [J/mol/K]) and $W$ is the molecular weight in [kg/kmol]. Equations of state that have a pressure with a non-linear dependence on temperature will deviate from this.

When enthalpy is used, the internal energy is calculated using

$$
e = h - \frac{p}{\rho}
$$
(5.6)

> **NOTE:** By default the internal energy is limited so that the temperature is greater than 0. If "limitT" is set to "no" the temperature and energy will not be limited. Caution should be used with this option.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models

text:
Internal energy is calculated using a constant value of specific heat at constant volume.

$$
e_T(T) = C_v(T - T_{ref}) + E_{s,ref}
$$
(5.7)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_v$ | Specific at constant volume [J/kg/K] |
| $T_{ref}$ | Reference temperature [K] (293.15 K default) |
| $E_{sref}$ | Reference sensible internal energy [J/kg/] ($T_{ref} C_v$ default) |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.1 eConst

text:
Internal energy is calculated using polynomial with powers of T.

$$
e_T(T) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} C_{v,i}T^i
$$
(5.8)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_v$Coeffs<8> | Specific heat at constant volume polynomial coefficients |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
| $S_f$ | Standard entropy [J/kg/K] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.2 ePolynomial

text:
Internal energy using a power function of temperature.

$$
e_T(T) = C_v(T)T
$$
(5.9)

$$
C_v(T) = C_0 \left( \frac{T}{T_{ref}} \right)^{n_0}
$$
(5.10)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_0$ | Reference heat capacity at constant volume [J/kg/K] |
| $n_0$ | Exponent of the power function |
| $T_{ref}$ | Reference temperature [K] |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.3 ePower

text: The incompressible tabulated thermodynamic model can be used to calculate the temperature using temperature to lookup the internal energy. The data is read from a one dimensional table. The specific heat are calculated using finite difference derivatives to the tables. See Sec. 12.1 for more information on the available options for modifiers and interpolation schemes. The "x" and "f" names are "T" and "e" respectively. A heat of formation, "Hf", must also be provided.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.4 eIcoTabulated

text:
The tabulated thermodynamic model can be used to calculate the temperature using density and temperature to find internal energy. The data is read from a two dimensional table. The specific heat are calculated using finite difference derivatives to the tables. See Sec. 12.1 for more information on the available options for modifiers and interpolation schemes. The "x", "y", and "f" names are "rho", "T", and "e" respectively. A heat of formation, "Hf", must also be provided.

> **NOTE:** The equation of state contribution of internal energy is not included so this must be included in the tables provided.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.5 eTabulated

text:
Enthalpy is calculated using a constant value of specific heat at constant pressure.

$$
h_T(T) = C_p(T - T_{ref}) + H_{s,ref}
$$
(5.11)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_p$ | Specific at constant pressure [J/kg/K] |
| $T_{ref}$ | Reference temperature [K] (293.15 K default) |
| $H_{sref}$ | Reference sensible enthalpy [J/kg/] ($T_{ref} C_p$ default) |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.6 hConst

text:
Enthalpy is calculated using polynomial with powers of T.

$$
h_T(T) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} C_{p,i}T^i
$$
(5.12)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_p$Coeffs<8> | Specific heat at constant pressure polynomial coefficients |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
| $S_f$ | Standard entropy [J/kg/K] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.7 hPolynomial

text:
Internal energy using a power function of temperature.

$$
h_T(T) = C_p(T)T
$$
(5.13)

$$
C_v(T) = C_0 \left( \frac{T}{T_{ref}} \right)^{n_0}
$$
(5.14)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $C_0$ | Reference heat capacity at constant volume [J/kg/K] |
| $n_0$ | Exponent of the power function |
| $T_{ref}$ | Reference temperature [K] |
| $H_f$ | Heat of formation [J/kg] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.8 hPower

text: The incompressible tabulated thermodynamic model can be used to calculate the temperature using temperature to lookup the enthalpy. The data is read from a one dimensional table. The specific heat are calculated using finite difference derivatives to the tables. See Sec. 12.1 for more information on the available options for modifiers and interpolation schemes. The "x" and "f" names are "T" and "h" respectively. A heat of formation, "Hf", must also be provided.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.9 hIcoTabulated

text:
The tabulated thermodynamic model can be used to calculate the temperature using density and temperature to find enthalpy. The data is read from a two dimensional table. The specific heat are calculated using finite difference derivatives to the tables. See Sec. 12.1 for more information on the available options for modifiers and interpolation schemes. The "x", "y", and "f" names are "rho", "T", and "h" respectively. A heat of formation, "Hf", must also be provided.

> **NOTE:** The equation of state contribution of internal energy is not included so this must be included in the tables provided.

text:
The JANAF thermodynamic model can be used in which the enthalpy is represented by a temperature based polynomial (OpenCFD Ltd., 2018b). Seven coefficients must be specified for both the low temperature and high temperature states, as well as the high, low, and switching temperatures. Currently, this model is only available for ideal gases.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `highCpCoeffs` | High enthalpy coefficients |
| `lowCpCoeffs` | Low enthalpy coefficients |
| $T_{low}$ | Minimum temperature [K] |
| $T_{common}$ | Switching temperature [K] |
| $T_{high}$ | Maximum temperature [K] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.1 Thermodynamic models 5.1.11 JANAF

text: In order to more easily handle a variety of equations of state, both temperature-based equations of state and internal energy based equations of state (e.g. in Mie-Grüneisen form) can be used.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states

text:
For a solid phase, it is assumed to have a constant density, $\rho_0$, and maintains a reference pressure $p_{ref}$. Because a solid thermodynamic model is never used to transport mass, the reference pressure is arbitrary and therefore set to 0 [Pa] by default.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $\rho_0$ | reference density [ kg/m³ ] |
| $p_{ref}$ | Reference pressure [Pa ] (default 101235 Pa) |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.1 rhoConst

text:
The Mie-Grüneisen form uses two contributions to calculate the pressure, and ideal gas term contribution, and a deviation term.

$$
p = (\Gamma_i - 1)\rho_i e - \Pi_i
$$
(5.15)

$\Gamma_i$, also called the Grüneisen coefficient, and $\Pi_i$ is the pressure deviation from an ideal gas and is specific to the equation of state. Using these quantities, the speed of sound is written as

$$
c^2_i = \frac{\Gamma_i p + \Pi_i}{\rho_i} - \delta_i(\Gamma_i - 1)
$$
(5.16)

where $\delta_i$ is defined

$$
\delta_i = \frac{-[p + \Pi_i]\Gamma'_i}{[\Gamma_i - 1]^2} + \frac{\Pi'_i}{\Gamma_i - 1}
$$
(5.17)

and where $\Gamma'_i$ and $\Pi'_i$ are the derivatives with respect to the phase density.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form)

text:
For an ideal gas, the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = (\gamma_i - 1)\rho_i e_i
$$
(5.18)

The functions as defined to represent an ideal gas in Mie-Grüneisen form are:

$$
\Gamma_i = \gamma_i
$$
(5.19)

$$
\Pi_i = 0
$$
(5.20)

$$
\delta_i = 0
$$
(5.21)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.1 idealGas

text:
For a material obeying the stiffened EOS, the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = (\gamma_i - 1)\rho_i e_i - \gamma_i a_i
$$
(5.22)

where $a_i$ and $\gamma_i$ are material properties (Zheng et al., 2011). In the Mie-Grüneisen form

$$
\Gamma_i = \gamma_i
$$
(5.23)

$$
\Pi_i = \gamma_i a_i
$$
(5.24)

and

$$
\delta_i = 0
$$
(5.25)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `a` | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.2 stiffenedGas

text:
The linear Tillotson equation of state was presented by (Wardlaw et al., 1998), and the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = p_{0,i} + \omega_i\rho_i(e_T - e_{0,i}) + A_i\mu + B_i\mu^2 + C_i\mu^3
$$
(5.26)

where $A_i$, $B_i$, $C_i$, and $\omega_i$ are material coefficients, and $p_{0,i}$ and $e_{0,i}$ are the reference pressure and internal energy. $\mu$ is defined as $\rho_i/\rho_{0,i} - 1$. The cavitation pressure, $p_{cav}$ is used as the minimum pressure which occurs when the density is sufficiently below the reference density.

In the Mie-Grüneisen form

$$
\Gamma_i = \omega_i + 1
$$
(5.27)

and

$$
\Pi_i = \omega_i\rho_i e_{0,i} - p_{0,i} - A_i\mu - B_i\mu^2 - C_i\mu^3
$$
(5.28)

and

$$
\delta_i = \frac{e_{0,i} - A + 2B\mu + 3.0C\mu^2}{\rho_{0,i}\omega_i}
$$
(5.29)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $p_0$ | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| $e_0$ | Reference internal energy [kJ/kg] |
| `omega` | Model coefficient [ ] |
| $A$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $B$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $C$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| `pCav` | Cavitation pressure [Pa] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.3 linearTillotson

text:
The Tillotson equation of state was originally developed for metals by Tillotson (1962), and the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = \max\left( \rho_i e\left( a + \frac{b}{\frac{e}{e_{0,i}\eta^2} + 1} \right) + A_i\mu + B_i\mu^2, p_{cav} \right)
$$
(5.30)

where $A_i$, $B_i$, $C_i$, and $\omega_i$ are material coefficients, and $p_{0,i}$ and $e_{0,i}$ are the reference pressure and internal energy (Wardlaw et al., 1998). $\mu$ is defined as $\rho_i/\rho_{0,i} - 1$. The cavitation pressure, $p_{cav}$ is used as the minimum pressure which occurs when the density is sufficiently below the reference density.

In the Mie-Grüneisen form

$$
\Gamma_i = a_i x + \frac{b_i e_{0,i}\rho_i^2}{x} - \frac{b_e e_{0,i}(\rho_i\rho_{0,i})^2}{x^2} + 1
$$
(5.31)

where

$$
x_i = e\rho^2_{0,i} + e_{0,i}\rho^2_i
$$
(5.32)

and

$$
\Pi_i = -A_i\mu - B_i\mu^2 - b_i\frac{(e\rho_i\rho_{0,i})^2 e_{0,i}\rho_i}{(e\rho^2_{0,i} + e_{0,i}\rho^2_i)^2}
$$
(5.33)

and $\delta_i$ is calculated using (5.17)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| $e_0$ | Reference internal energy [kJ/kg] |
| `a` | Model coefficient [ ] |
| `b` | Model coefficient [ ] |
| $A$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $B$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| `pCav` | Cavitation pressure [Pa] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.4 Tillotson

text:
For a material obeying the stiffened EOS, the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = (\gamma_i - 1)\rho_i e_i - \gamma_i(b_i - a_i)
$$
(5.34)

where $a_i$, $b_i$, and $\gamma_i$ are material properties (Zheng et al., 2011). In the Mie-Grüneisen form

$$
\Gamma_i = \gamma_i
$$
(5.35)

$$
\Pi_i = \gamma_i(b_i - a_i)
$$
(5.36)

and

$$
\delta_i = 0
$$
(5.37)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `a` | Material parameter [Pa] |
| `b` | Material parameter [Pa] |
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.5 Tait

text:
For a gas described by the generalized van der Waals equation of state (Zheng et al., 2011), the pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = \frac{\gamma_i - 1}{1 - b_i\rho_i}(\rho_i e_i + a_i\rho^2_i) - (a_i\rho^2_i + c_i)
$$
(5.38)

Putting the pressure in the Mie-Grüneisen form, we obtain

$$
\Gamma_i = \frac{\gamma_i - 1}{1 - b_i\rho_i} + 1
$$
(5.39)

$$
\Pi_i = \left( 1 - \frac{\gamma_i - 1}{1 - b_i\rho_i} \right)a_i\rho^2_i + \left( \frac{\gamma_i - 1}{1 - b_i\rho_i} + 1 \right)c_i
$$
(5.40)

and

$$
\delta_i = -b_i\frac{p_i + a_i\rho^2_i}{\gamma_i - 1} + \left( \frac{1 - b_i\rho_i}{\gamma - 1} - 1 \right)2a_i\rho_i
$$
(5.41)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `a` | Attraction between particles [kg⁻¹ m⁵ s⁻²] |
| `b` | Specific volume excluded due to particle volume [kg⁻¹ m³] |
| `c` | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.6 vanderWaals

text:
The Landau, Stanyukovich, Zeldovich, and Kompaneets equation of state is a simple model for describing an ideal explosive (Lutzky, 1964; Needham, 2018). It takes a form similar to a stiffened gas or Tait EOS, with

$$
\Gamma_i = \gamma_i
$$
(5.42)

$$
\Pi_i = a_i\rho^{b_i}_i
$$
(5.43)

and

$$
\delta_i = 0
$$
(5.44)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `a` | Model constant [kg¹⁻ᵇ s⁻² m³ᵇ⁻¹] |
| `b` | Pressure exponent [ ] |
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.7 LSZK

text:
The more complicated Jones Wilkins Lee EOS is often used to define energetic materials (Zheng et al., 2011), and has a pressure deviation given by

$$
\Pi_i = A_ie^{-R_{1,i}V}\left( \frac{\omega_i}{R_{1,i}V} - 1 \right) + B_ie^{-R_{2,i}V}\left( \frac{\omega_i}{R_{2,i}V} - 1 \right) - \rho_i\omega_ie_{0,i}
$$
(5.45)

where $V = \rho_{0,i}/\rho_i$.

$$
\Gamma_{r,i} = \omega_i + 1
$$
(5.46)

and

$$
\delta_{r,i} = A_ie^{-\frac{R_{1,i}\rho_{0,i}}{\rho_i}}\left[ \omega_i\left( \frac{1}{R_{1,i}\rho_{0,i}} + \frac{1}{\rho_i} \right) - \frac{R_{1,i}\rho_{0,i}}{\rho_i^2} \right]\frac{1}{\omega_i} + B_ie^{-\frac{R_{2,i}\rho_{0,i}}{\rho_i}}\left[ \omega_i\left( \frac{1}{R_{2,i}\rho_{0,i}} + \frac{1}{\rho_i} \right) - \frac{R_{2,i}\rho_{0,i}}{\rho_i^2} \right]\frac{1}{\omega_i} - e_{0,i}
$$
(5.47)

> **NOTE:** The JWL model can also be used to describe the unreacted state if a detonating model is used with the `solidJWL` type. For the solid case, $e_{0,i}$ is calculated so that there is zero pressure at the reference density, and uses an offset pressure, "pRef". Thermal energy is also not considered for the solid case

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $A$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $B$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $R_1$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| $R_2$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| `rho0` | Unreacted or reference density [kg m⁻³] |
| `omega` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |
| $e_0$ | Offset energy (0 by default for gas) [J/Kg] |
| `pRef` | Offset pressure (only for solid, 0 by default) [Pa] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.8 JWL

text:
The Cochran Chan EOS can be used to describe a solid material (Zheng et al., 2011), and has a reference pressure given by

$$
p_{ref,i} = A_iV_i^{1-E_{1,i}} - B_iV_i^{1-E_{2,i}}
$$
(5.48)

The functions used to defined the Mie-Grüneisen equations are

$$
\Gamma_i = \Gamma_{0,i} + 1,
$$
(5.49)

$$
\Pi_i = \Gamma_{0,i}\rho_i\left( -\frac{A_i}{(E_{1,i} - 1)\rho_{0,i}}V_i^{1-E_{1,i}} + \frac{B_i}{(E_{2,i} - 1)\rho_{0,i}}V_i^{1-E_{2,i}} - e_{0,i} \right) - p_{ref,i}
$$
(5.50)

and

$$
\delta_i = \frac{A_i}{E_{1,i}}\left[ \frac{E_{1,i}V_i^{-E_{1,i}}}{E_{1,i} - \Gamma_{0,i} - 1}\frac{1}{\rho_i} + \frac{\Gamma_{0,i}}{\rho_{0,i}} \right]\frac{1}{\Gamma_{0,i}} + \frac{B_i}{E_{2,i}}\left[ \frac{E_{2,i}V_i^{-E_{2,i}}}{E_{2,i} - \Gamma_{0,i} - 1}\frac{1}{\rho_i} + \frac{\Gamma_{0,i}}{\rho_{0,i}} \right]\frac{1}{\Gamma_{0,i}} - e_{0,i}
$$
(5.51)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $A$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $B$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $E_1$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| $E_2$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| `Gamma0` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |
| $e_0$ | Reference energy (0 by default) [J/Kg ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.9 CochranChan

text:
The Doan-Nickel EOS includes changes in the composition of air at high temperatures and the changing specific heat ratio due to dissociation of molecules Doan and Nickel (1963). Due to the way this model is defined, it can currently only be used with inviscid fluids and a constant specific heat at constant volume (eConst). The specific heat is a function of the density and internal energy and is defined as

$$
\Gamma_i = 1 + \left( 0.161 + 0.255e^{\tilde{e}/e_1}f_1 + 0.280e^{\tilde{e}/e_2}(1 - f_1) + 0.137e^{\tilde{e}/e_3}f_2 + 0.050f_3 \right) \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{\alpha(\rho_i,\tilde{e})}
$$
(5.52)

where $\tilde{e} = e \cdot 10^{-6}$. $e_1 = 4.46$, $e_2 = 6.63$, and $e_3 = 25.5$ are the internal energies at which oxygen dissociates, everything is dissociated, and electrons contribute, respectively. $\rho_{0,i}$ is the density of air at sea-level (1.293 [kg/m³], and

$$
\alpha(\rho_i, \tilde{e}) = [0.048f_1 + 0.032(1 - f_1)(1 - f_2)]\log_{10}(\tilde{e}) + 0.045f_3
$$
(5.53)

with

$$
f_1 = \frac{1}{\exp\left( \frac{\tilde{e} - e_{O_2\to 2O}}{\Delta e_{O_2\to 2O}} \right) + 1}
$$
(5.54)

$$
e_{O_2\to 2O} = 8.5 + 0.357\log_{10}\left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)
$$
(5.55)

$$
\Delta e_{O_2\to 2O} = 0.975\left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{0.05}
$$
(5.56)

$$
f_2 = \frac{1}{\exp\left( \frac{e_{N_2\to 2N} - \tilde{e}}{\Delta e_{N_2\to 2N}} \right) + 1}
$$
(5.57)

$$
e_{N_2\to 2N} = 45.0\left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{0.0157}
$$
(5.58)

$$
\Delta e_{N_2\to 2N} = 4.0\left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{0.085}
$$
(5.59)

$$
f_3 = \frac{1}{\exp\left( \frac{e_e - \tilde{e}}{\Delta e_e} \right) + 1}
$$
(5.60)

$$
e_e = 160.0
$$
(5.61)

and

$$
\Delta e_e = 6.0
$$
(5.62)

Due to the complexity of the model, and the fact that it was specifically developed as a model for air, all coefficients are hard-coded and cannot be changed. This equation of state should only be used to represent standard air.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.2 Internal energy based (Mie-Grüneisen form) 5.2.2.10 DoanNickel

text:
While it is preferable to use an internal energy based equation of state for compressible flows, some equations of state cannot be converted, and therefore use the local temperature to define the thermodynamic pressure. Generally the Grüneisen coefficient used to calculate the shared pressure is defined as

$$
\Gamma_i = \frac{v_i}{C_v}\frac{\partial p}{\partial T}
$$
(5.63)

where $C_v$ is the specific heat at constant volume, and the speed of sound is defined

$$
c^2_i = v^2_i\left[ \left( \frac{\partial p_i}{\partial T} \right)^2 \frac{T}{C_v} - \frac{\partial p}{\partial v_i} \right]
$$
(5.64)

Unless otherwise specified, these relations are used to calculate the relevant quantities.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based

text:
The perfect gas equation of state uses the standard ideal gas pressure relation, however the specific heat ratio is not held constant, allowing for the use of non-constant heat capacity models.

$$
p_i = RT\rho_i
$$
(5.65)
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.1 perfectGas

text:
The C-form of the Jones Wilkins Lee equation of state (Souers et al., 2000) does not have a dependence on the temperature or internal energy and has a pressure defined as

$$
p_i = A_ie^{-R_{1,i}V} + B_ie^{-R_{2,i}V} + \frac{C_i}{V^{1+\omega_i}}
$$
(5.66)

the speed of sound if defined

$$
c^2_i = \frac{V^2}{\rho_{0,i}}\left( A_ie^{-R_{1,i}V} + B_ie^{-R_{2,i}V} + \frac{C_i(1 + \omega_i)}{V^{2+\omega_i}} \right)
$$
(5.67)

The Grüneisen coefficient is the same as the standard JWL equation of state.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $A$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $B$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $C$ | Model coefficient [Pa] |
| $R_1$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| $R_2$ | Model coefficient [ ] |
| `rho0` | Unreacted or reference density [kg m⁻³] |
| `omega` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.2 JWLC

text:
The equation of state of Abel-Nobel is commonly used for modeling simulate explosive materials, specifically for propellants (Johnston, 2005). Unlike the JWL equation of state, the BKW models uses the temperature, rather than the internal energy, to define the pressure.

$$
p_i = \frac{RT\rho_i}{1 - b_i\rho_i}
$$
(5.68)

where $b$ is the co-volume of the fluid.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `b` | Co-volume [m³/kg ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.3 AbelNobel

text:
The Becker-Kistiakowsky-Wilson equation of state is another equation of state that is commonly used to simulate explosive materials (Mader, 1963). Unlike the JWL equation of state, the BKW models uses the temperature, rather than the internal energy, to define the pressure.

$$
p_i = RT\rho_i\left( 1 + xe^{\beta x} \right)
$$
(5.69)

where

$$
x = \frac{\kappa k\rho_i}{W_i(T + \theta)^a}
$$
(5.70)

and $W_i$ is the molecular weight in [kg/kmol].

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `beta` | Model coefficient [ ] |
| `a` | Temperature exponent [ ] |
| `Theta` | Model coefficient [K] |
| `kappa` | Model coefficient [Kᵃ] |
| `k` | Specie co-volume [m³/kmol] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.4 BKW

text:
The Benedict-Webb-Rubin equation of state was developed by (Benedict et al., 1942) to describe real gases using a set of eight coefficients that must be experimentally determined. The pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = RT\rho_i + \left( B_0RT - A_0 - \frac{C_0}{T^2} \right)\rho^2_i + (bRT - a)\rho^3_i + a\alpha\rho^6_i + \frac{c\rho^3_i}{T^2(1 + \gamma\rho^2_i)}e^{-\gamma\rho^2_i}
$$
(5.71)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| $A_0$ | Model coefficient |
| $B_0$ | Temperature exponent |
| $C_0$ | Model coefficient |
| `a` | Model coefficient |
| `b` | Model coefficient |
| `c` | Model coefficient |
| `alpha` | Model coefficient |
| `gamma` | Specific heat ratio [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.5 BWR

text:
The Murnaghan (or Munahan) equation of state is used for solid material and has no temperature dependence (Souers et al., 2000). The pressure is a function of only the density and is defined as

$$
p_i = p_{ref} + \frac{1}{\kappa n}\left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} - 1 \right)^n
$$
(5.72)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `pRef` | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| `kappa` | Model coefficient (1/K0) [Pa⁻¹] |
| $K_0$ | Bulk modulus (can be used in place of $\kappa$) [Pa] |
| `n` (or $K_0$) | Model coefficient (default 1) [ ] |
| `Gamma` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.3 Temperature-based 5.2.3.6 Murnaghan

text: The tabulated equation of state can be used to calculate the pressure using the density and temperature. The data is read from a two dimensional tables. See Sec. 12.1 for more information on the available options for modifiers and interpolation schemes. The "x", "y", and "f" names are "rho", "T", and "p" respectively.
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.4 tabulatedEOS

text:
The second order Birch-Murnaghan equation of state is the second order expansion of the Birch-Murnaghan model. The pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = p_{ref} + \frac{3K_0}{2K'_0}\left[ \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{7/3} - \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{5/3} \right]
$$
(5.73)

Many coefficients can be found for this in Zheng and Zhao (2016).

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `pRef` | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| $K_0$ | Bulk modulus [Pa] |
| `Gamma` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |
title: Fluid and solid thermodynamic models 5.2 Equation of states 5.2.4 tabulatedEOS 5.2.4.1 BirchMurnaghan2

text:
The Third order Birch-Murnaghan equation of state is the third order expansion of the Birch-Murnaghan (see Zheng and Zhao (2016)). The pressure is defined as

$$
p_i = p_{ref} + \frac{3K_0}{2K'_0}\left[ \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{7/3} - \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{5/3} \right] \times \left( 1 + 0.75(K'_0 - 4)\left[ \left( \frac{\rho_i}{\rho_{0,i}} \right)^{2/3} - 1 \right] \right)
$$
(5.74)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `pRef` | Reference pressure [Pa] |
| `rho0` | Reference density [kg/m³] |
| $K_0$ | Bulk modulus [Pa] |
| `K0Prime` | Change in bulk modulus w.r.t. pressure [ ] |
| `Gamma` | Grüneisen coefficient [ ] |

text: The transport models are used to define quantities such as viscosity and thermal diffusion. Only Newtonian viscosity models are currently available. All transport models, with the exception of the tabulated methods ported from OpenCFD Ltd. (2018b).

text:
Constant values for viscosity ($\mu$) and Prandtl number are used.

$$
\kappa = \mu C_p/Pr
$$
(5.75)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `mu` | Dynamic viscosity [Kg/m/s] |
| `Pr` | Prandtl number [ ] |

text:
Viscosity is calculated using Sutherland's formula for viscosity

$$
\mu(T) = \frac{A_s\sqrt{T}}{1 + T_s/T}
$$
(5.76)

$$
\kappa = \mu C_v\left( 1.32 + \frac{1.77R}{C_v} \right)
$$
(5.77)

text:
Transport package using polynomial functions of the natural logarithm of temperature for the natural logarithm of dynamic viscosity and thermal conductivity:

$$
\log(\mu(T)) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} \mu_i(\log(T))^i
$$
(5.78)

$$
\log(\kappa(T)) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} \kappa_i(\log(T))^i
$$
(5.79)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `muCoeffs<8>` | Dynamic viscosity coefficients |
| `kappaCoeffs<8>` | Conductivity coefficients |

text:
Transport package using polynomial functions of temperature for the dynamic viscosity and thermal conductivity:

$$
\mu(T) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} \mu_iT^i
$$
(5.80)

$$
\kappa(T) = \sum_{i=0}^{7} \kappa_iT^i
$$
(5.81)

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `muCoeffs<8>` | Dynamic viscosity coefficients |
| `kappaCoeffs<8>` | Conductivity coefficients |

text:
Transport package using the Williams-Landel-Ferry model for viscosity of polymer melts (Williams et al., 1955):

$$
\mu(T) = \mu_0\exp\left( \frac{-C_1(T - T_r)}{C_2 + T - T_r} \right)
$$
(5.82)

$$
\kappa(T) = \frac{C_p(T)\mu(T)}{Pr}
$$
(5.83)

| `Pr` | Prandtl number [ ] |
